entries.name: The St Thomas Christians — Two Obediences
entries.informalName: The Thomas Christians Between Rome and Antioch
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on two texts the community wrote itself, one for each party. Its window opens in 1665, where the entry on the Coonan Cross ends, and closes in 1815. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing:
Strong for this window. The Library holds two texts by the community itself, printed in English in 1873. One is a history kept by the Malankara party, whose date is unknown. The other is the Angamaly document of 1787, from the party that kept to Rome.

An English chaplain's book of 1873 and a British visitor's account of 1806 add outside views. No Malayalam original has been read.
entries.floorNote: No question. The Malankara party's own history says Mar Evanius taught "that Christ has one nature and that the Holy Ghost is equal with the Father and the Son". The other party stood under Rome.
entries.relationsSummary:
This entry carries on the church of the Coonan Cross. After 1665 its people took two roads. One party took bishops from Antioch. The other kept to Rome, under Carmelite bishops at Verapoly.

A bishop of the Church of the East came once, in 1708. The Mar Thoma reform of 1836 grew inside the Antioch party.
entries.why: In 1665 a bishop sent from Antioch reached Malabar. By his hands, the community's own history says, its leader Mar Thomas the Great "was lawfully consecrated". Part of the community went with Antioch, and part stayed with Rome. In 1787 delegates of eighty-four churches wrote that in future they would have no bishop but one of their own.
entries.teaser: The Malabar coast, 1665 to 1815 — one ancient church under two sets of bishops, and a paper of 1787 that said: no bishop but our own.
entries.longDescription:
In 1653 the Thomas Christians swore at Mattancherry that they would have nothing more to do with the Jesuits. They chose Archdeacon Thoma as their Metran. He had been named only, not consecrated. In 1665 a bishop named Mar Gregorius arrived, sent from Antioch. Mar Gregorius laid hands on Mar Thomas the Great. The community's own history says he "was lawfully consecrated".

Two parties formed. In the words of the Malankara party's own history, one was the Old Christians, who are Roman Catholics, and the other the New Christians, who are Syrians. The pope sent Carmelite bishops to Verapoly to govern the Old Christians.

More bishops came from the east. In 1678, says the same history, Mar Basilius and Mar Evanius arrived. Evanius "re-established our former church services" and taught the Trinity and one nature in Christ. A priest of Kottayam, writing in 1869, dates the coming of Mar Evanius to 1685.

In 1708 a bishop called Gabriel came "by the direction of Mar Alea". The text calls him a Nestorian bishop, a name for the Church of the East. He taught that the Messiah has two natures, and "much dispute arose". Some Syrians and some Roman Catholics joined him.

After he died, the history says, those who joined him returned to their former parties. A list of the bishops in the same book says he died at Kottayam in 1731.

In 1751, the history says, a patriarch and two bishops came from Syria. For nineteen years they disputed with the Syrians. Then letters from Antioch made Mar Thomas a Metropolitan, as Mar Dionysius. The list of bishops dates the three bishops to 1761 and the consecration to 1772.

On 1 February 1787 delegates of eighty-four churches met at Angamaly.

The English chaplain Whitehouse calls them Romo-Syrians. That means Syrians in union with Rome. Their paper blames two orders, the Carmelites and the Jesuits. It says they "oppressed our forefathers in various ways". In future, it says, "we will have no Bishop but from among ourselves". If the Queen of Portugal refused, they would turn to the Chaldean Patriarch.

In 1806 the British visitor Claudius Buchanan met the Metropolitan at Kandanad. His name was Mar Dionysius. Buchanan wrote that the old man told him he had come "to visit a declining Church". The list of bishops says Mar Dionysius died about 1814.

entries.name: Chinese Catholics Under Edict and Treaty
entries.informalName: The Church of the Court and the Provinces
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on Rome's rulings, a Jesuit's letter and one Catholic encyclopedia of 1908. Its window runs from 1650, where the Ming China entry ends, to 1906, where the twentieth-century entry begins. Almost nothing in it comes from Chinese hands. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing:
Good for the eighteenth century, thinner for the nineteenth.

Almost every text is a missionary's or a Roman office's.

The sources are Roman rulings, a Jesuit's letter, and a Catholic book of 1908.

The Chinese edicts and memorials come only in the missionaries' translations.

No text by a Chinese Catholic has been read.
entries.floorNote: No question. This is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed. The Rites dispute was about practice, not the creed.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry carries on the church the Jesuit mission began in Ming China. It tells the Jesuits at the court, the Rites quarrel and the church of the provinces. Priests of the Paris Foreign Missions Society served in its provinces from about 1680. The twentieth-century entry carries its story on from 1906.
entries.why: For two and a half centuries the Catholic Church in China lived by the favor of the court and the text of edicts. Rome argued over whether Chinese Christians could honor Confucius and their dead. In 1724 an edict sent nearly every missionary out of the provinces. Treaties of the 1840s and 1860s then opened the country again.
entries.teaser: China, 1650 to 1906: a church that served the court, split Rome over Confucius and outlived a ban.
entries.longDescription:
The Jesuit mission of the Ming years went on at the Qing court. The Jesuits served the emperor as astronomers and interpreters. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1908 says they stood high in favor. In March 1692, it adds, a note from the president of the Board of Rites said it seemed unfair to ban the Europeans' religion. An imperial decree approved the note. Copies went to all the provincial governors.

The Rites quarrel asked what a Chinese Christian might do for Confucius and the dead. In 1645 missionaries in China sent questions to Rome. The Holy Office answered them on 23 March 1656. It let Chinese Christians join the rite in the Confucius hall. It seemed, the ruling says, to be worship that is only civil and political.

In 1658 Rome named two French priests, Pallu and Lambert de la Motte, to lead the missions of China. The seminary they asked for was given a site in Paris in 1663 and opened in 1664. The encyclopedia calls it the beginning of the Paris Foreign Missions Society.

Propaganda wrote to them in 1659. It asked what could be more absurd than to carry France, Spain or Italy into China.

Rome later turned against the rites.

Father Ricci was the Jesuits' first leader in China. He was tolerant of the Chinese rites, the encyclopedia says. Rome, not China, decided the question. Maigrot was a vicar apostolic in Fujian and a priest of the Paris Foreign Missions. In 1693 he condemned the rites in a mandate. A bull of Benedict XIV settled the matter on 11 July 1742. It was, the encyclopedia says, "a terrible blow to the missions in China".

In 1723 officials in Fujian asked the emperor to send the Europeans out of the provinces. Europeans at the court could stay.

On 16 October 1724 the Jesuit de Mailla wrote from Peking. He said the holy faith was entirely banned in China. Churches were pulled down or turned to common uses. An order of 1723 complained of girls who were kept from marriage and called virgins.

The church went on in the provinces. In 1726 Propaganda ruled that Chinese-born priests must swear the same oath as the Europeans. In 1736 an edict of the Ch'ien-lung emperor forbade the preaching of Christian doctrine on pain of death. A persecution in Fujian in 1746 killed Bishop Sanz and four Spanish Dominicans.

In 1755 Propaganda warned the missionary at Peking for letting Mass be said in Chinese on feast days. It forbade the practice for the future. In 1766 the Holy Office was told that Christians in China were few and could not avoid their non-Christian neighbors' tables. It allowed them to eat food set before them, even if offered to idols, outside any temple and with no sign of worship.

In 1811 a decree ordered a search for foreign preachers. In 1844 a treaty was signed at Whampoa. On 20 February 1846 the emperor ordered that the old Christian buildings be restored.

Treaties in 1858 and 1860 gave missions special privileges. These were the Treaty of Tientsin and the Peking Convention. Anger followed in 1870. A Holy Office instruction of the 1860s dealt with trouble in Hunan. Non-Christians, it says, were angry at a treaty and drew crosses on the roads so that Christians had to step on them. At Tientsin on 21 June 1870, twenty-one people died, among them a Lazarist and a Chinese priest named Hu.

The Boxer rising of 1900 brought "sad days for the missions". The encyclopedia says five bishops were among the dead.

The governor-general and viceroy of Fujian — who asked in 1723 that Europeans leave the provinces
entries.legacy: The church outlived the edicts. Its story goes on in the entry on Chinese Catholicism after 1906.

entries.name: Japan's Hidden Christians
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) as a gap in the story, but the evidence is thin. Its window runs from 1650, where the Kirishitan entry ends, to 17 March 1865, where the next entry begins. The village communities speak only through a French historian of 1896. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Adequate, and almost all from one source. The French historian Marnas told the story in 1896, from the missionaries' letters. He is an outsider and a Catholic writer. The communities' own book has not been found in Japanese. It is called Tenchi hajimari no koto, the Beginning of Heaven and Earth.
entries.floorNote: No dated statement of belief by the communities has been read. They are treated as the Kirishitan church carried on in hiding, and that church clears the floor. In 1865 the missionaries found the Creed among the prayers they kept, in old Japanese. Whether the later Kakure still hold the creed is a question for the next entry.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry carries on the Kirishitan church that the ban of 1614 drove underground. It ends on 17 March 1865, when villagers at Urakami told Father Petitjean that their hearts were the same as his. The next entry takes up the story from that day. The Paris Foreign Missions Society, Marnas wrote, was the body that found them.
entries.why: In 1666, Marnas says, Edo ordered an inquiry in every town and village. It asked what each family believed. Once a year every Japanese had to trample a cross or a holy picture. In 1865, Marnas says, most villages had a chief of prayer and a baptizer. Later studies hold that the hidden believers kept the faith for about 250 years without a priest.
entries.teaser: Japan, 1650 to 1865 — village churches that kept baptism and prayer for more than two centuries under a ban.
entries.longDescription:
In 1614 Japan banned Christianity, and the entry before this one tells how it began. Marnas wrote the history of the church's return in 1896. He says that in 1666 the government at Edo set up an inquiry in every town and village to learn what each family believed. Once a year, he adds, every Japanese had to tread on a cross laid on the ground, or on an image of the Virgin and the saints.

This was the e-fumi, the treading of the image. Marnas says its inventors meant it to expose the surviving Christians or force them to give up the faith.

Almost everywhere the hidden Christians kept the same order, Marnas says. Most villages had two chiefs. The chief of prayer led the Sunday prayers and went to the dying.

The baptizer gave baptism and trained a pupil to take his place. Marnas credits these offices, oral teaching and a few kept books and images for the survival of the faith.

In 1865 the missionaries studied the papers the villagers had kept.

They included prayer books, written baptism formulas and Christian calendars.

One treatise, Contrition, was dated 1603 and written wholly in Japanese. The baptizer Domingo brought it to the missionaries. It had escaped a search at Urakami eight years before. Then twenty-eight Christians were jailed and most of their books were burned. On 17 March 1865, at about half past twelve, twelve to fifteen people stood at the door of the church of the Twenty-Six Martyrs in Nagasaki.

Three women knelt beside Father Petitjean. One said, with her hand on her heart, that the hearts of all of them were the same as his. Then she asked, "Sancta Maria no gozowa doko?", "Where is the image of Holy Mary?" (our rendering). Within weeks the missionaries counted about 3,800 Christians.

About 1,300 lived at Urakami and 2,500 in the hills and on the nearby islands.
voices: Bernard Petitjean — the French priest at Nagasaki who met the Urakami villagers on 17 March 1865
Domingo — a village baptizer who brought the missionaries the treatise Contrition in 1865
entries.legacy: The next entry takes up their story on 17 March 1865. Some of the villagers, the Kakure, chose to stay apart from the visible church.
entries.peopleNote: The Library holds no words of their own from the hidden Christians, so no one is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through Japanese Christianity after 1906, by way of the next entry on the villagers who came forward in 1865. The tree rates the descent thin, because no text from inside the communities covers these years.

set.longDescription:
On 17 March 1865, weeks after a French church opened in Nagasaki's foreign settlement, a group of villagers from nearby Urakami came in, and one woman quietly told the priest that the hearts of all present were the same as his, and asked where the statue of Mary was. They were descendants of Christians driven underground in the 1600s, who had kept baptism, prayers and a liturgical calendar for over two hundred years without a single priest. In the months that followed tens of thousands more made themselves known. The government's ban was still in force, and the Urakami villagers were deported and held until 1873. When it was lifted, a Christianity of three kinds grew quickly in Meiji Japan. Catholic parishes rebuilt around the emerging hidden communities, Protestant bands of samurai-class students at Yokohama, Kumamoto and Sapporo, and a Russian Orthodox mission that Nikolai of Japan had begun in 1861 and staffed largely with Japanese clergy. Not all the hidden Christians rejoined: some, the Kakure, kept the tradition exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.

The priests who met them belonged to the Paris Foreign Missions Society. In his history of the church's return, Marnas wrote in 1896 that this Society found the descendants of the old Christians in 1865. He said it was born long ago from the inspiration of Alexandre de Rhodes.

sources.note: A French Catholic historian who writes from the missionaries' letters; read in a public-domain copy for the Paris Foreign Missions Society line only.

set.longDescription:
Korea is the only country in the world where the Catholic Church began without a missionary. In the late eighteenth century a circle of Confucian scholars near Seoul studied Chinese-language Catholic books, convinced themselves, and sent one of their number, Yi Sung-hun, to Beijing to be baptized in 1784. He came home and baptized the others, and a church of several thousand people existed before a priest had ever set foot in the country. It was written in Korean from the start — Chong Yak-chong's catechism was in the vernacular script rather than in the scholarly Chinese of the elite. Which is part of why it reached women, servants and the poor as fast as it reached the literati. The Choson state read it as treason against the Confucian order, and the church spent a century under persecution, with something on the order of ten thousand Korean Catholics killed in successive purges between 1801 and 1866, until a treaty with France in 1886 finally brought the killing to an end.

The Paris Foreign Missions Society had an establishment in Korea.

In 1866, says the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1908, two bishops and seven priests of the Society were beheaded in March. Only three priests of the Society were left, it says: Ridel, Féron and Calais.

sources.note: This is the lay church teaching itself, in its own hand. The attribution of the Essence of Sacred Doctrine to Yi Byeok is debated among scholars. English-language access is chiefly through Baker and Rausch's translations.

sources.note: A believer's appeal written on silk during the Sinyu persecution, intercepted by authorities. It survives only in the persecutors' own archive, and it combines genuine faith testimony with a politically sensitive appeal for foreign intervention - both parts of the record, without softening either.
